Question
========
In a set associative cache, we use some bits of the address as a row index. These bits are the ones next to the offset bits.

What happens if we use the most significant bits instead, when we iterate over consecutive data?


Answerlist
----------
* We will have more contention
* We will have less contention
* We will be able to store less data
* We will be able to store more data

Solution
========
Consecutive data differs only in the least significant bits. If the row index is taken from the most significant bits, a whole run of consecutive addresses maps to the same row, so the ways of that single row are the only usable entries and they evict each other.

Answerlist
----------
* 1. Consecutive addresses share their most significant bits, so they all land in the same row and fight for the same few ways.
* 0. The opposite happens: accesses concentrate on one row instead of spreading over all rows.
* 0. The physical capacity of the cache is unchanged; only the distribution of the accesses changes.
* 0. The physical capacity of the cache is unchanged.
